doc.title: Frank Foster and Bill Hughes interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Schenectady, New York, March 28, 1995

chapter: Oral tradition, teaching and Shiny Stockings
title: Shiny Stockings, and Hughes's Magic solo
summary: Foster tells how his first wife's stockings inspired the chart and how Basie liked it after a poor Philadelphia rehearsal; Hughes notes his Magic solo, a Frank Wess blues.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Yeah. I have to ask you about “Shiny Stockings.” I mean that’s a great piece. Can you remember how’d that thing start?
It was a pair of shiny stockings.
Tell us the story behind that.
Well see now this involves my first wife and I’m not inclined to talk, speak too well of her.
Tell us about the chart.

Okay, the chart was inspired by my first wife putting on stockings. This was in 1954 BPH (before panty hose), when stockings were really stockings. You know and all the appendages, yes garter belts, I didn’t want to say it. But and she used to put them on and the light would hit her legs in a certain way. And it just, the phrase “Shiny Stockings” just came to me, looking at this repeatedly, repeatedly, you know. Something happens long enough to you and you get an idea about it. And so I put it into a song. But the really significant part of the history of that song was that I labored over the arrangement, I made sure that every note was just right, in the right place. And the first time we rehearsed it was in Pep’s Bar in Philadelphia. And we had come in that day and the band was tired and evil, and everybody wanted to get some rest and nobody felt like rehearsing. And I just can’t for the life of me figure why Basie insisted on this rehearsal. But customarily we rehearsed the first day, the opening day in any club that was a week or two weeks or more, we rehearsed the first day of the engagement. Well this first day, no one felt like rehearsing and I brought “Shiny Stockings” in. And the way the guys felt was manifested in the way they played this song. And I said oh God, this will never be played because if something didn’t sound good in rehearsal, Basie nixed it. It just wouldn’t get played. “Shiny Stockings” did not sound good in that first rehearsal, but Chief must have heard

something there, he must have realized that, well the guys are all evil and tired, and they’re not putting their hundred percent, but there’s something in there. He must have. Because that’s one of the few charts that I ever contributed that Basie years later came to me and said, “hey, Foss, that ‘Shiny Stockings,’” he said, “you really put one down that time.”
That’s exactly the way he would have said that too.
And of course that’s like a standard now. Everybody plays it everywhere. You know if you’re like a college big band and you haven’t played “Shiny Stockings” you don’t know the repertoire.
That must make you feel good, doesn’t it.
Certainly. Yes it does. It makes me feel very good.

Like I think about guys trying to tell guitar players to do a certain thing. You’re doing a swing tune and you say, “now do that Freddie Green thing.” I mean that’s such a contribution that’s something to be really proud of.
I did that in rehearsal today — to Steve Promise.
Did he know what you were talking about?
Yes.
And you did a solo, what’s that tune “Magic” that you played on?
Yeah, that was a blues that Frank Wess, Frank Wess wrote that. That’s what we used to call him—
Still is his nickname.
No kidding, I’ll have to remember that when we see him.
Yeah, and every now and then I got a chance to stand up from Frank. But that’s a long time ago.
